title: My own work
hookLine: better one's own duty done imperfectly than another's done well (Bhagavad Gita 3.35)

cards: Scrolling at midnight, and everyone else's work looks better. The friend who started a bakery. The cousin who travels for her job.
The stranger whose desk is a beach. Some nights a person can spend more energy wishing for someone else's path than walking their own. The Bhagavad Gita has a line for that.

This block has already met Arjuna between two armies, ready to drop his bow. By the third chapter, his charioteer Krishna is still answering him, and the answer turns to a question of whose work is whose.

teach.b: First, the line itself, in the third chapter of the Gita.
In paraphrase: better your own duty, even done imperfectly, than another's duty done well. The Sanskrit word is svadharma, your own dharma, your own duty or path. Second, the surprise.
The verse doesn't say do your own work well. It says your own work done badly is better than someone else's done brilliantly. Krishna isn't praising sloppiness.

He's saying something about where a person belongs. Borrowed work, even when it looks good, isn't yours, and the verse goes further: another's duty is full of danger. Third, Hindus read this in more than one way.
Some older commentators tied your own duty to your place in society, the duties of your family and station.
Some modern readers hear it more as your own nature: the gifts, temperament and responsibilities that are actually yours, not the ones you envy.
Both readings are found among Hindus today, and teachers can disagree sharply about the first. Fourth, the ordinary version. A parent trying to raise their children the way another family does.
A coworker doing someone else's job because it's more visible. An artist copying a style that isn't theirs.
The Gita's question is quiet and hard: what's actually mine to do?
By the end of the Gita, Arjuna says he will do as Krishna asks. On an ordinary day the duty in front of us is usually smaller: an email, a dish, a conversation we've been avoiding.

how: Hindus read and recite the Bhagavad Gita at home and in temples and study groups; Gita 3.35 is often taught as a call to do one's own duty faithfully rather than imitate another's.

o: a duty you take on to earn praise from others
your own duty or path, even done imperfectly
the one law that applies the same to everyone

games.q: you're Arjuna. the duty in front of you is hard, and walking away looks cleaner. what does Krishna tell you?
o: take up whatever path looks best done.
your own duty, even imperfect, is better than another's done well.
leave all work and go to the forest.
games.why: Gita 3.35: better one's own duty done imperfectly than another's done well. by the end of the Gita, Arjuna says he will do as Krishna asks.

practice: Bring to mind someone whose work or life you've quietly wished were yours, without scolding yourself, then gently set it down, like putting someone else's coat back on the hook.
Ask what's in front of you that only you can do, a person who needs you in particular, a task that's yours, and let it come into focus, small or unfinished as it may be.
If you pray, you can offer that work in your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: Svadharma. The Gita's word for your own duty: better your own, done imperfectly, than another's done well. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit, from the Hindu tradition (Bhagavad Gita 3.35): your own dharma, your own duty or path.

carryVoice: Your line: imperfect, and our own. Borrowed work, however good it looks, isn't ours. See you tomorrow.
